html:
Aurel Stein (1862 to 1943) was a Hungarian-born British archaeologist who explored the lost Buddhist towns of the Silk Road in the Tarim Basin of Xinjiang. Working from British India, he made four expeditions between 1900 and 1930.

He dug at Khotan, Niya, Miran and Loulan, towns buried by the sands of the Taklamakan, and found wooden tablets in Kharosthi script, paintings and silks. In 1907 at the Mogao caves near Dunhuang, he persuaded the Taoist caretaker Wang Yuanlu to sell him thousands of manuscripts from a sealed library cave, among them the Diamond Sutra of 868, the oldest dated printed book. They are now in the British Library and the British Museum.

In Britain he was knighted and honoured; in China he is remembered as a plunderer, and the Chinese government stopped his fourth expedition in 1930. His finds, with those of Sven Hedin and others, brought the forgotten history of the Silk Road back to light. He died in Kabul at 80, about to begin work in Afghanistan.
